etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hacche, hache, from Old English hæċ, from Proto-West Germanic *hakkju (compare Dutch hek ‘gate, railing’, Low German Heck ‘pasture gate, farmyard gate’), variant of *haggju ‘hedge’. More at hedge.

definitions.definition: A horizontal door in a floor or ceiling.
A trapdoor.
An opening in a wall at window height for the purpose of serving food or other items. A pass through.

quote.citation: 1950 June, “New Restaurant and Buffet Cars, G.N.R.(I.)”, in Railway Magazine, page 415:
quote.text: A service hatch with sliding shutter is situated at the end of the kitchen next to the dining compartment.

definitions.definition: A small door in large mechanical structures and vehicles such as aircraft and spacecraft often provided for access for maintenance.

quote.citation: 1963 February, “Diesel locomotive faults and their remedies”, in Modern Railways, page 100:
quote.text: A surprising number of incidents is due to roof hatches being left loose or in the raised position when locomotives return to service after maintenance. On one occasion, a 25kV overhead line was damaged by an open hatch.

definitions.definition: (nautical) An opening through the deck of a ship or submarine
(slang) A gullet.
A frame or weir in a river, for catching fish.
A floodgate; a sluice gate.

quote.citation: 1879, Richard Jeffries, Wild Life in a Southern County:
quote.text: The farmers lower down the brook pull up the hatches to let the flood pass.

definitions.definition: (Scotland) A bedstead.

quote.citation: 1819 December 20 (indicated as 1820), Walter Scott, Ivanhoe; a Romance. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh:  […]  Archibald Constable and Co.; London: Hurst, Robinson, and Co. […], →OCLC:
quote.text: It consisted of a rude wooden stool , and still ruder hatch or bed-frame

definitions.definition: (mining) An opening into, or in search of, a mine.
(transitive) To close with a hatch or hatches.

quote.citation: c. 1607–1608, William Shakeſpeare, The Late, And much admired Play, Called Pericles, Prince of Tyre. […], London: Imprinted at London for Henry Goſſon,  […], published 1609, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: 'Twere not amiss to keep our door hatched.

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English hacche, hacchen (“to propagate”), from Old English *hæċċan, āhaċċian (“to peck out; hatch”), from Proto-Germanic *hakjaną.

Cognate with German hecken ‘to breed, spawn’, Danish hække (“to hatch”), Swedish häcka (“to breed”); akin to Latvian kakale ‘penis’.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of young animals) To emerge from an egg.
(intransitive, of eggs) To break open when a young animal emerges from it.
(transitive) To incubate eggs; to cause to hatch.
(transitive) To devise (a plot or scheme).

quote.citation: 2017 August 27, Brandon Nowalk, “Game Of Thrones slows down for the longest, and best, episode of the season (newbies)”, in The Onion AV Club‎[1]:
quote.text: As for Cersei, pretending to work with her enemies while secretly hatching some grander scheme was pretty much what I expected for the truce going into it.

definitions.definition: The act of hatching.
(figurative) Development; disclosure; discovery.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i], page 266:
quote.text: There's ſomething in his ſoule? / O'er which his Melancholly ſits on brood, / And I do doubt the hatch, and the diſcloſe / Will be ſome danger, which to preuent / I haue in quicke determination

definitions.definition: (poultry) A group of birds that emerged from eggs at a specified time.
(often as mayfly hatch) The phenomenon, lasting 1–2 days, of large clouds of mayflies appearing in one location to mate, having reached maturity.

quote.citation: a. 1947, Edward R. Hewitt, quoted in 1947, Charles K. Fox, Redistribution of the Green Drake, 1997, Norm Shires, Jim Gilford (editors), Limestone Legends, page 104,
quote.text: The Willowemoc above Livington Manor had the largest mayfly hatch I ever knew about fifty years ago.

quote.citation: 2004, Ed Engle, Fishing Small Flies‎[2], page 118:
quote.text: The major application of the parachute is for mayfly hatches, but it's also useful for midge hatches.

quote.citation: 2007, John Shewey, On the Fly Guide to the Northwest‎[3], page 70:
quote.text: Many years the mayfly hatch begins by the time the lake opens in April. Otherwise, expect strong hatches by mid-May. The hatches continue through midsummer.

definitions.definition: (informal) A birth, the birth records (in the newspaper).

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French hacher (“to chop, slice up, incise with fine lines”), from Old French hacher, hachier, from Frankish *hakōn, *hakkōn, from Proto-Germanic *hakkōną (“to chop; hack”). More at hack.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To shade an area of (a drawing, diagram, etc.) with fine parallel lines, or with lines which cross each other (cross-hatch).

quote.citation: 1695, C[harles] A[lphonse] du Fresnoy, translated by John Dryden, De Arte Graphica. The Art of Painting, […], London:  […]  J[ohn] Heptinstall for W. Rogers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Those hatching strokes of the pencil.

quote.citation: [1611?], Homer, “(please specify |book=I to XXIV)”, in Geo[rge] Chapman, transl., The Iliads of Homer Prince of Poets. […], London:  […]  Nathaniell Butter, →OCLC; republished as The Iliads of Homer, Prince of Poets, […], new edition, volume (please specify the book number), London: Charles Knight and Co., […], 1843, →OCLC:
quote.text: Shall win this sword, silvered and hatched.The spelling has been modernized.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To cross; to spot; to stain; to steep.
